children: OTTAWA--Retail spending by Canadians looks to have remained on the rise last month, though the pace is showing signs of cooling as uncertainty and gasoline prices remain high.

The value of retail trade in the country increased 1.2% in August from the previous month to a seasonally adjusted 74.57 billion Canadian dollars, the equivalent of about US$53.23 billion, Statistics Canada said Friday. That was broadly in line with expectations and more than enough to recover from a 0.8% drop a month prior, the first fall in sales of the year.

Momentum looks to have carried into September, with the statistics agency's early estimate indicating sales for the month rose 0.7%. Statistics Canada offered no detail with the early tally of receipts, but with goods prices and the cost of fuel up again last month economists say retail volumes may have been flat.
The agency also estimated manufacturing sales in September rose an eighth month in the last nine, though with the value of shipments edging up 0.1% following growth of 1.5% the month before.

The data suggest a softer handoff for the economy entering the final quarter of the year and comes ahead of the Bank of Canada's monetary policy decision next week and possibly the first increase in interest rates after no change since a cut a year ago.

"The recent resilience in consumer spending will be tested this autumn as elevated gasoline prices and higher interest rates squeeze household incomes, while the population shrinks," said Tony Stillo, director of Canada economics at Oxford Economics. "Household discretionary spending will also be weighed down by the recent escalation in the U.S.-Canada trade war, which hurts job prospects and further raises uncertainty."

The sales survey for August showed broad growth among retailers, driven by activity at new car dealers and with higher gasoline prices lifting spending at the pumps. Compared with a year earlier, retail sales were up 5.4%. In volume terms, trade increased a similar 1.2% for the month and 1.8% compared with 2025.

That is in keeping with economist estimates the economy grew roughly 2% in annualized terms in the third quarter, weaker than the 3.3% pace recorded the period before but still solid compared with the sluggish 0.3% expansion in the first quarter of this year.
Statistics Canada's September forecast was based on the responses of fewer than 60% of retailers surveyed and will be revised.

Cardholder spending in September tracked by Royal Bank of Canada, the country's largest lender, showed that discretionary services remained the strongest category, and spending on gasoline was up sharply alongside a rise in fuel prices, but outlays on discretionary goods inched down. The bank calculated core sales, stripping out gasoline and autos, rose 0.4% on a three-month basis, slightly cooler than August's 0.6% growth.
For August, Statistics Canada said sales were up in all nine industry segments it tracks.

Sales at motor vehicle and parts dealers were up 1.2%, led by a rebound in new cars that countered a decline for used car dealers. Sales at gas stations and fuel vendors increased 1.7%, the first rise in three months, though the volume of sales dropped by 0.5%.

Core retail sales were up 1.1% between July and August after a fall of 0.7% a month prior, led by the first rise in three months for food and drink, a recovery at general merchandise retailers and continued growth at health and personal-care stores.

"The broad-based rise in retail sales in August largely reflects a rebound from July rather than a genuine strengthening in consumer demand, though there were still signs in the data that households are showing resilience amid higher gasoline prices. That will add to the Bank of Canada's concerns that weak demand is becoming less of a barrier to firms passing on higher energy costs, supporting a hike next week," said Bradley Saunders, North America economist at Capital Economics.
